newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea strikes start up again with weaker momentum.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea strikes start up again with weaker momentum.

text.p: Scores of South Korean unions resumed strikes on Friday after a New Year holiday break and an outlawed union umbrella body threatened to escalate unrest next week unless the government revoked a controversial labour law.
The leader of the militant Korean Confederation Trade Union (KCTU), Kwon Young-kil, told a news conference that the strikes would get worse if the union's demands were not met.

"If the government doesn't nullify the labour law, we will expand strikes into the Hyundai unions, construction unions and office workers unions on Monday, and on Tuesday the public sector unions, such as hospital unions, subway unions and broadcast unions," he said.
However, fewer unions heeded the confederation's call to action on Friday. The confederation, which claims a 500,000 membership, said about 90,000 workers from 43 unions resumed strikes on Friday.
That was down from a peak of 190 unions, encompassing about 230,000 workers, who walked out during the last week of December, according to the confederation.
The Labour Ministry said less than 20,000 workers from 26 unions joined the strike on Friday. Estimates by the ministry and union umbrella organisations have varied widely.
The more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the largest umbrella group, with 1.3 million members, postponed their strikes until after January 11.
The federation planned rallies for Sunday and the KCTU has announced a rally for Friday evening.

South Korea was engulfed in a wave of industry-crippling strikes in December when the ruling party, in a clandestine session of parliament, rammed through a labour law allowing companies to replace strikers, hire temporary staff and lay off workers.

The work stoppages, which hit Korea's ship building and automobile manufacturing industries as well as hospitals and subways, were postponed until after the New Year holidays to spare the public chaos.

The Kia Motors union said 18,000 workers went back on strike on Friday and would continue until the labour law was reversed. The company's public relations office said employees were on holiday and would be back to work on Monday.
The Daewoo Motor Co union was on a partial strike on Friday afternoon, and said it would hold a two-hour strike on Saturday morning. Plans for Monday were still undecided.
